The weekly routine

Friday closeAll decisions use closing prices of the last trading day of the week. Nothing is decided mid-week.
Data refresh (Saturday morning)Six index ETFs and the stocks of the picked index from Yahoo Finance; VIX, financial conditions, Sahm rule and yield curve from the Federal Reserve.
Pick the main indexScore the six ETFs by return per unit of risk; switch only if the best score is more than 0.25 ahead of the current pick.
Core buyThe weekly amount rule sets €40–€200, invested in the main index's ETF. This is the main strategy.
Extra profit (optional)Close last week's 3 longs and 3 shorts, open this week's from the picked index's stock ranking.
Record & reviewThe demo account books every result, and the 2012–today backtest is re-run each week.

You place the trades yourself at your broker; the site only decides and records.

The methods

Main index pick (weekly)core strategy: what to buy

Six euro-listed, accumulating index ETFs: MSCI World (EUNL), S&P 500 (SXR8), Nasdaq-100 (SXRV), MSCI Europe (EUNK), MSCI Japan (EUNN) and MSCI Emerging Markets (IEMA).

return(index) = Friday close ÷ close 52 weeks earlier − 1 (in euros, dividends included) risk(index) = standard deviation of weekly moves over 52 weeks × √52 score(index) = return ÷ risk (return per unit of risk) pick = best score if score(best) − score(current pick) > 0.25 = current pick otherwise

Twelve-month momentum across countries is one of the most replicated results in finance (Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen 2013); dividing by volatility ("risk-adjusted momentum") avoids jumping into the most volatile market just because it rose most. Until 11 Oct 2026 the rule used the 52-week return alone with a 5-point buffer; the variant table on the Index pick page shows why it changed.

Evidence

2012–today, weekly, real ETF prices in euros: pick —%/yr (worst fall —%) vs MSCI World —%/yr, S&P 500 —%/yr, Nasdaq-100 —%/yr; previous rule —%/yr. On 1990–2026 regional data (monthly, US dollars): pick —%/yr vs North America —%/yr and the developed world —%/yr. Full tables on the Index pick page.

How to follow it: put each week's money into the pick; keep what you already own when the pick changes. Selling everything on each switch is what the lump-sum figures assume; it triggers tax in a normal account.

Weekly buy amount (€40–€200)core strategy: how much

Buy more when the world market is cheaper than its record, less when it is near the top, never stop. Measured on the MSCI World ETF in euros (not on the pick, which by design is usually near its high). Money not spent in calm weeks stays with you; nothing waits in cash.

Rule (checked in this order)
TierCondition at the Friday closeBuy
StressMSCI World below its 40-week trend line and (Sahm rule ≥ 0.5 or Chicago Fed NFCI > 0) and VIX < 30€40
Bear market / panic20%+ below the record close, or VIX ≥ 30€200
Correction10–20% below the record€150
Dip5–10% below the record€100
NormalWithin 5% of the record€60
Evidence

2012–today on the MSCI World ETF: rule —%/yr vs flat —%/yr (money-weighted, same total). Over 100 years of US data (1927–today, drawdown tiers only): —% vs —% a year; never worse than a flat amount in any starting period tested. Small but consistent.

Budget

Since 2012 the rule averaged €— a week and asked for €150 or more in —% of weeks. A 2008-style crash can ask for €200 every week for many months.

Market meter (−100 … +100)market context

Six readings on the world market and US stress gauges (the US drives global credit and recessions), each scored −1 to +1, multiplied by a weight and summed: meter = 100 × Σ weight × score.

ComponentWeightScore
World trend25%clip((MSCI World ÷ 40-week line − 1) ÷ 5%, −1, +1)
Discount from record20%clip(−drawdown ÷ 15%, 0, +1): falls are bullish (contrarian)
Fear (VIX)15%≥ 30: +1 · 20–30: +0.5 · under 13: −0.5 (complacency) · else 0
Credit (Chicago Fed NFCI)15%above 0: −1 · −0.3 to 0: −0.3 · below −0.3: +0.3
Recession (Sahm rule)15%≥ 0.5: −1 · 0.3–0.5: −0.5 · below 0.3: +0.3
Yield curve (10Y − 3M)10%inverted: −0.5 · positive: +0.2

Labels: +40 or more very strong market, +15 to +40 strong, −10 to +15 mixed, −25 to −10 weak, below −25 very weak. Until 11 Oct 2026 they said "buy" and "sell"; the test below showed the readings don't predict returns, so they now only describe the market.

Evidence (weekly, 2012–today)

Average MSCI World return over the next 52 weeks by meter reading: mixed —%, strong —%, very strong —%. On 100 years of US data neither the trend nor the distance from the record predicted the next year either (correlation about 0). The meter is a description of the market, not a timing tool: that's why the demo account stays fully invested whatever it says. Valuation is left out: it predicts 10-year returns, not next week's.

Research: the 10/20/30% plans and the 200-day trend rulenot used by IndexPilot

Kept as research because you asked what 20% or 30% a year would take. Tested on the US market because it has 100 years of data and euro-listed 2x/3x funds. Trend line: the average of the last 200 daily closes (the weekly job uses the 40-week average of Friday closes, which tracks it within about 0.3%). Checked once a week at the Friday close.

PlanHoldsRule1990–2026Worst fall2017–26 daily
10% Steady1x S&P 500 ETFWeekly amount rule, never sell11.0%/yr−49%14.8%/yr
20% Growth2x daily-leveraged ETFHold above the trend line, cash below16.4%/yr−38%18.9%/yr
30% Aggressive3x daily-leveraged ETPSame rule17.9%/yr−58%25.3%/yr

Share of 10-year spans that reached the target: 48% (10% plan), 15% (20%), 0% (30%; best 29.0%/yr). Without the trend rule, 3x lost 99% between 2000 and 2009. About 3 sell/buy-back switches a year.

100-year test (1927–2026, monthly total returns): 1x hold 10.3%/yr, worst fall −84% · 2x + trend rule 11.1%/yr, worst fall −86% · 3x + trend rule 6.8%/yr, worst fall −99.7%. Crashes inside one month (1929–32, May 1940, October 1987) defeat the trend rule. A volatility brake did not fix it (3x still fell about −90%). The leveraged plans are shown for comparison; the evidence does not support them.

Market gaugesinputs to the amount and meter

Nine US readings from the Federal Reserve, refreshed every weekday: VIX (fear), yield curve 10Y−3M, Sahm rule, unemployment, high-yield credit spread, Chicago Fed financial conditions (NFCI), Fed funds rate, 10-year yield and CPI inflation. Each gets a status from its usual professional threshold (VIX ≥ 30 panic, curve below 0 recession warning, Sahm ≥ 0.5 recession signal, high-yield spread above 5 pp stress, NFCI above 0 tight conditions). They are US measures because US recessions and credit stress hit every market; the world market's own trend and distance from its record come from the MSCI World ETF.

Timing tested: on 1990–2026 US data, no rule that paused buying on these warnings beat plain steady buying; money waiting in cash cost more than the crashes avoided. So they change how much you buy, never whether you stay invested.

Stock ranking of the picked indexstock picks, extra profit
Main indexStocks rankedMethod
S&P 500All S&P 500 members with complete data (~486)Value + momentum (below)
Nasdaq-100The 100 membersPrice momentum
MSCI EuropeEURO STOXX 50 + the 30 largest UK, Swiss and Nordic companiesPrice momentum
MSCI JapanNikkei 225 membersPrice momentum
MSCI Emerging MarketsThe 50 largest emerging-market companiesPrice momentum
MSCI WorldAll of the above lists combinedPrice momentum
price momentum score = 50% × rank(return from 12 months ago to 1 month ago) + 50% × rank(position in 52-week range)

Outside the US there is no free, reliable source of company fundamentals, so those rankings use prices only. Stocks with a 1-year move over +300% are flagged for checking. The lists of members are reviewed once a year.

S&P 500 version (value + momentum)

Scored within each sector, so banks are compared with banks and tech with tech.

value = 50% × rank(earnings ÷ price) + 25% × rank(sales ÷ price) + 25% × rank(book ÷ price) momentum = rank(position in 52-week range: (price − low) ÷ (high − low)) score = 50% × value + 50% × momentum (0–100; ranks are sector percentiles)

Loss-making companies get the lowest earnings rank. P/E under 6 is flagged as a likely data error. Value and momentum are the two factors with the strongest academic record (Fama-French, AQR), and they work best combined because they tend to move in opposite directions.

Demo account and the Extra profit recordsimulation

Demo account (€1,000 a week, long only): €1,000 is deposited at every Friday close; profits stay in. 70% in the main-index ETF (switched only with the pick; new money tops it up to 70%; trimmed only above 80%). 30% in the 3 highest-ranked stocks of that index, split by inverse volatility; a stock is kept while it stays in the top 20% and is sold if it drops out, falls 25% below its highest close since purchase, or the main index changes. 0.2% cost per trade; stock values converted to euros at Yahoo Finance exchange rates. Benchmark: the same deposits put into the MSCI World ETF on the same days.

Why this mix: on 100 years of US data, holding the strongest 10% of stocks by 12-1 month momentum beat the market in every period tested, before costs: —%/yr vs —% since 1927 and —% vs —% since 2007. The 70/30 mix keeps most of the index's diversification: —%/yr since 2007. Adding shorts lowered the worst fall but, the money tied up in shorts cost more return than it added (—%/yr). Timing the index with the meter and leverage were left out because they lost in the tests.

Extra profit record: separate paper record of the weekly picks: long the 3 highest-ranked stocks and short the 3 lowest-ranked (skipping flagged data), opened at the Friday close and closed at the next. Each side is split by inverse volatility: weight = (1 ÷ volatility) ÷ Σ(1 ÷ volatility), using each stock's last 12 months of daily moves. Results are in % of the stake (half long, half short), so they apply to any amount. No costs. Record starts 9 Oct 2026.

How everything was testedmethodology
  • No look-ahead: each decision uses only data available before it is acted on (previous month or previous Friday).
  • Total return: the ETFs are accumulating, so their prices already include reinvested dividends. The US research uses Kenneth French total returns.
  • Leveraged funds (monthly test): monthly return = L × index − (L − 1) × cash rate − (L² − L) ÷ 2 × variance − fee, with variance from the VIX. This reproduces the daily-reset drag of real 2x/3x funds. Fees 0.07% (1x), 0.6% (2x), 0.75% (3x) a year.
  • Daily check: the plans were re-run day by day on Federal Reserve data for Jul 2017–Oct 2026 with weekly decisions, as you would actually trade them.
  • Measures: yearly growth rate, money-weighted return (each euro counted from when it went in), worst fall from a peak, worst calendar year, rolling 10-year returns, profit per euro staked.
  • Known bias: the 1990–2026 data uses monthly average prices, which smooths falls; real drawdowns were somewhat deeper. Thresholds were chosen with this history in view, which flatters results.
Risk managementbuilt in and up to you
  • Diversified core: the main strategy is always a whole index fund (hundreds of companies), bought every week.
  • Slow switching: the buffer keeps the pick in place unless the lead is clear; about 1–2 changes a year.
  • Budget cap: €40–€200 a week; know that crashes ask for the maximum for many months.
  • No leverage: the research plans show why: near-total losses in the 1930s and 1940.
  • Position size: leveraged plans and the extra-profit trades only with money you could see halve (or worse).
  • Shorts: can lose more than the stake; consider a stop-loss or skip them.
  • Not modelled: taxes on each sale, spreads and broker fees. The ETF tests are in euros; the US and regional research is in dollars.

Limits and honest caveatsread this
  • Backtests describe the past; the future can be worse. Results are before tax.
  • The index pick's 2012–today edge came mostly from holding the Nasdaq-100; on 35 years of regional data it did not beat holding North America.
  • No rule here has reliably beaten plain, steady buying of the index; the gains from the weekly amount rule are small.
  • The 20% and 30% plans did not reach their targets over 1990–2026, and over 100 years they suffered near-total losses.
  • The stock picks are untested historically; judge them by the live record over months, not weeks.
  • The site is a personal research tool, not financial advice. You make and place every trade yourself.
